templates.title: Build a swipe file of winning UGC ads in my category
templates.outcome: A reference library of 30 high-performing UGC examples with hook breakdowns
templates.prompt:
Build me a swipe file of 30 high-performing UGC ads in [category] from TikTok and Instagram.

Find them in the platforms' ad libraries, in the creators' own feeds where the post is labelled as a paid partnership, and by watching what keeps reappearing in the feeds of accounts that follow our category. Only include things that are actually ads, and only ones where I can see they performed — high view counts relative to the creator's normal posts, or long-running placements in the ad library, which is the strongest signal there is because nobody keeps paying for an ad that does not work.

For each one, write into a Google Doc: the link, the brand, the creator, the platform, how long it has been running or its view count, and a breakdown:

The hook — the first three seconds, transcribed word for word, plus what is on screen. Transcribe it exactly; paraphrasing the hook loses the thing worth stealing.
The structure — what happens in what order, with timestamps.
The proof — how they make the claim believable.
The CTA — what it is and how hard it lands.
Why it works.

Then group them by hook pattern at the end, so the file is browsable by problem rather than being thirty entries in the order you found them.

templates.title: Tear down a competitor's social strategy
templates.outcome: A report on their cadence, formats, and what works that you can act on
templates.prompt:
Tear down [competitor]'s social strategy on Instagram and TikTok. I want something I can act on, not a list of observations.

Go through their last [90] days on both platforms and work out:

Cadence — how often they post, on what days and at what times, and whether that has changed.

Formats — the mix, with rough percentages. Which formats they use for which purpose.

What actually works for them — their top posts by engagement relative to their own median, and what those have in common. Their worst performers too; what a competitor has tried and abandoned is as useful as what they keep doing.

Voice and positioning — how they talk about themselves, what claims they lean on, who they are implicitly talking to.

Production — how much each post plausibly costs to make. A strategy that needs a full-time editor is not a strategy we can copy.

Then the part I actually need: three things they are doing that we should, one thing they are doing that we should deliberately not, and one gap in their coverage we could take.

Use their real numbers throughout, and say when you are estimating. And do not conclude that something works for them just because they do a lot of it — plenty of accounts post the same failing format for a year.

templates.title: Write personalized collab DMs for my creator list
templates.outcome: A draft DM for every creator on your list, grounded in their actual content
templates.prompt:
Open my creator list at [sheet link] and write a collab DM for each one.

Before writing anything for a creator, look at their last ten posts. The message has to reference something specific and recent from their actual content — a post, a series they run, a bit they do, something they said. If it could be sent to any creator in the niche, it is not ready.

The DM: under 400 characters. Open with the specific thing. Say who we are in half a sentence. Say what the collab is concretely — [product, paid, affiliate, gifted, whatever it is] — because a vague "let's collaborate" wastes their time and gets ignored. Close with one easy question.

Do not open with "Hi [name], love your content!" Do not call it an exciting opportunity. Do not mention their follower count.

Write each draft into the sheet next to the creator, along with the specific post you built it on, so I can check the reasoning rather than just the message.

Where a creator's recent content makes them a bad fit — they just did a deal with a competitor, they have shifted niche, the audience is wrong — say so in the row and skip the draft rather than writing something I should not send.

Drafts only. Nothing sends.

templates.title: Mine YouTube comments for content ideas in my niche
templates.outcome: A ranked list of content ideas pulled from what viewers actually ask for
templates.prompt:
Mine the comments on the most-watched videos in [niche] for content ideas.

Take [10-15] popular videos from the last [6] months in the niche and read their comment sections properly — sorted by top and by newest, since those surface different things. Cross-reference against what people are asking about the same topic on X.

What I am looking for: questions the video did not answer, disagreements with what the creator said, "but what about" comments, people describing their specific situation and asking how it applies, and requests for a follow-up.

Group them into themes rather than listing individual comments. Twenty people asking variations of the same question is one content idea with strong demand behind it, and that is the thing worth knowing.

For each theme: the question in plain terms, how many comments across how many videos raised it, two or three representative quotes with links, whether anyone has already made the video that answers it, and a suggested title and angle.

Rank by demand and by how badly the existing content covers it. A question asked constantly that nobody has answered well is the whole point of this exercise.

Ignore spam, bot comments, and the generic praise that makes up most of any comment section.

templates.title: Track viral posts about my topic on X every day
templates.outcome: A daily shortlist of breakout posts with ready-to-edit reply and quote drafts
templates.prompt:
Every day at noon, find the posts about [topic] on X that are breaking out, and draft something I could say about them.

Breaking out means unusual for that account — a post doing 20x what the author normally does is more interesting than a big account's normal Tuesday. Only the last [12] hours; joining a conversation a day late is joining nothing.

For each of the [3-5] worth my attention: the link, the author and who they are, the post text, the numbers, and what is actually driving it — is it a genuinely good point, a controversy, a well-made claim that happens to be wrong, or a joke.

Then draft two things for each: a reply and a quote post. The reply should add something specific from my experience with [my domain]. The quote post should have a real position in it — agreement with a reason, a counterpoint, or a piece of context the thread is missing.

Never draft something that just agrees enthusiastically. Never draft a reply that pivots to my product; the ones that work are the ones that are about the topic.

And where a post is breaking out because it is a pile-on or because someone is being attacked, say so and do not draft anything. Drafts only.

templates.title: Pick a fair giveaway winner from my post comments
templates.outcome: A verified winner plus backup picks and a clean audit trail of all entries
templates.prompt:
Pick the winner of my giveaway from the comments on [Instagram post link]. The entry rules were [rules — e.g. follow the account, tag a friend, comment].

Collect every comment on the post with the username, the text, and the timestamp, and check each against the rules. Someone who did not tag anyone did not enter; someone who tagged four people in four comments entered once, not four times, unless the rules said otherwise.

Then filter out entries that should not be in the pool: accounts created in the last [30] days, accounts with no posts and no followers, giveaway-farming accounts that enter hundreds of these, and duplicate accounts run by the same person where that is evident. Say how many you removed and why, as a group — the credibility of the draw rests on that number being visible.

Write the full audit trail to a sheet: every comment collected, whether it qualified, and the reason if not.

Then pick one winner and [3] backups from the valid pool, using a method you state explicitly — the index selected, out of how many, and how the ordering was fixed. A draw nobody can reproduce is one somebody will accuse me of rigging.

Do not announce anything, do not DM anyone, do not comment on the post.

templates.title: Audit my profiles and links across every platform
templates.outcome: A punch list of dead links, stale bios, and mismatches across your profiles
templates.prompt:
Audit my presence across LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok [and any others I list] and give me a punch list of what is broken or stale.

Check every link first: bio links, link-in-bio pages and everything on them, links in pinned posts, links in the About section. Follow each one and report its actual status — 200, redirect chain, 404, dead domain, parked page, or a page that loads but no longer says what it used to. A link that quietly started redirecting to a marketing homepage instead of the thing I meant is the kind of thing that survives for a year.

Then consistency: is the profile photo the same across platforms, is the name written the same way, does the bio describe the same thing, is the current role right everywhere. Quote what each one says so I can see the drift.

Then staleness: anything mentioning a company I have left, an old title, an event that has passed, a product we renamed, a launch that shipped.

Give me a punch list ordered by how bad it is — a dead link on my most-visited profile first, an inconsistent capitalisation last. One line each: platform, what is wrong, what to change it to.

Read only. Do not edit any profile.

templates.title: Get a Slack digest when creators I track post
templates.outcome: A daily Slack message summarizing net-new posts from your watchlist
templates.prompt:
Every morning, check my watchlist at [link — YouTube channels, subreddits, creators] for anything new in the last 24 hours and post a digest to [Slack channel].

Net-new only. Keep track of what has already been reported so the same video does not appear three mornings running because it is still on the channel page.

For each new item: who posted it, the title, the link, how long it is or how long it takes to read, and two or three sentences on what it actually says. Not the description they wrote — what is in it. The whole value of a digest is that the reader can decide from the summary whether to open it.

Flag anything that mentions us, a competitor, or [key topics], and put those at the top of the message.

Keep the Slack message tight: a bold line per source, bullets under it, links inline. If it runs long, cut the least important items and say how many you cut rather than posting a wall nobody reads.

If nothing new appeared, post one line saying so. A silent day is information, and a digest that only posts when there is news makes people wonder whether it broke.

templates.title: Write an SEO content brief for a keyword
templates.outcome: An outline with target terms, headings, and links a writer can run with
templates.prompt:
Write an SEO content brief for [keyword] and put it in a Google Doc.

Start with the search results. Read the top [10] pages properly and tell me what they have in common: the format they take, how long they are, what sections they all include, and what search intent they are all serving. That last one settles everything else — a keyword whose results are all comparison pages does not want a how-to guide, however good the guide is.

Then the brief:

Target keyword, the related terms and questions that appear across the results and in People Also Ask, and the intent in one sentence.

A recommended angle — what we can do that the top ten do not. If the honest answer is that the results are already comprehensive and we would be the eleventh identical page, say that; it is worth more than a brief for a piece that will never rank.

An outline: H1, then every H2 and H3 with a line on what goes under it, in an order that answers the query fastest.

What to include — the specific data, examples, screenshots or original material that would make this better than what exists.

Internal links from our site, external sources worth citing, a title tag and meta description, and a target word count with the reasoning.

templates.title: Build a press list and draft pitches
templates.outcome: Targeted journalists with beats, contacts, and a personalized pitch each
templates.prompt:
Build me a press list for [story — the launch, funding, research, whatever it is] and draft a pitch for each journalist.

Find journalists who have actually written about [topic / this space] in the last [12] months. Recency and beat are everything: a reporter who covered our space two years ago and has since moved to another beat is a wasted send, and they remember the ones who did not check.

For each: name, publication, their beat in their own words if their bio states it, two or three recent relevant pieces with links and dates, their contact route (email if published, otherwise the outlet's tips address or their social), and their location.

Then draft the pitch, one per journalist, and make each genuinely different. Reference a specific piece they wrote and why our story connects to it. Subject line under [60] characters and specific. Then: what the story is in two sentences, why it matters to their readers, what we can offer (data, an interview, an exclusive, early access), and one line on who we are. Under 200 words total.

No embargoes or exclusives promised to more than one person — say explicitly which pitch offers what.

Write the list to a Google Sheet with the drafts. Nothing sends. And do not put an email address in the sheet that you guessed from a name pattern.

templates.title: Vet creators before a partnership
templates.outcome: An audience-quality and brand-fit scorecard for each creator you're eyeing
templates.prompt:
Vet [creator handles] before we do a partnership. Build a scorecard for each in a Google Sheet.

Audience quality first, because this is where the money is lost. Look at their last [15] posts and calculate engagement from actual numbers rather than a media kit. Check whether engagement scales with reach or sits suspiciously flat. Read the comments: real comments about the content, or emoji strings and generic praise from accounts with no posts. Check the follower growth curve for step changes that look bought. Check whether the audience geography and language match where we sell.

Then brand fit: what they actually post about, the proportion that is sponsored (a feed that is half ads converts badly), which brands they have worked with, and whether any of those are our competitors or in categories we would not want to sit next to.

Then risk: anything in their history that would be a problem for us, and how they have handled controversy. Say what you found and where, without editorialising.

Score each dimension with the evidence beside it, and give a recommendation: go, go with conditions, or no. Where the numbers do not add up but nothing is provable, say "the pattern is consistent with purchased engagement" rather than either accusing them or ignoring it.

templates.title: Write ad copy variations to test
templates.outcome: On-brand ad variations across distinct angles, hooks, and CTAs
templates.prompt:
Write ad copy variations for [product] to test on [platform]. The audience is [who], the offer is [what], and the format needs [character limits / structure]. Our brand voice is [description, or: see examples at link].

Give me [4] distinct angles, not four rewrites of the same sentence. Variations that all say the same thing differently produce a test that teaches nothing. Make them genuinely different bets:

One on the problem — name the pain sharply enough that the right person recognises themselves.
One on the outcome — what life looks like after, concretely.
One on proof — a number, a named result, a specific customer situation.
One that is a real contrarian take on how people usually solve this.

For each angle: three hook or headline options, the body copy, and two CTA options. Say in a line what hypothesis that angle is testing, because that is what I read the results against.

Write it into a Google Doc grouped by angle.

Stay inside the character limits exactly — copy that gets truncated mid-sentence in the feed is a wasted variation. Make no claim I have not given you evidence for, and flag anything that would need legal or substantiation review before it runs.

templates.title: Scrape this directory into a spreadsheet
templates.outcome: A clean, deduplicated CSV of every entry with pagination handled
templates.prompt:
Scrape [directory URL] into a spreadsheet.

Work out how the listing paginates before you start — numbered pages, infinite scroll, a load-more button, or a URL parameter — and handle it properly. Getting the first page and stopping is the most common way this fails, and it fails silently because the output looks fine.

For each entry capture [fields — e.g. name, category, location, website, phone, description]. If the useful fields only exist on the detail page rather than the listing, open each detail page.

De-duplicate on [the field that is actually unique — website domain or phone, not name] and say how many duplicates you collapsed.

Clean as you go: consistent casing, phone numbers in one format, URLs with the scheme, empty rather than "N/A" or "-" for missing values.

Write it to a Google Sheet, one row per entry, with the source URL of each detail page as the last column so any row can be checked.

Tell me the count you expected from the directory's own total and the count you got. If those disagree, say so and say why rather than handing me a sheet that is quietly missing a third of the listings. If the site blocks automated access or the terms forbid it, stop and tell me instead of working around it.

templates.title: Research missing fields for every row in my sheet
templates.outcome: Your sheet filled in with researched data and a source link for each value
templates.prompt:
Open [sheet link]. Some columns are filled and [these columns] are empty. Research and fill them in.

For each row, use what is already there to identify the subject unambiguously first. Filling in a field for the wrong company is worse than leaving it blank, and it is the failure mode that never gets caught.

For each value you find, write the value and put the source URL in the adjacent [Source] column. A number without a source is a number I have to verify myself, which means the row saved me nothing.

Where sources disagree, use the most authoritative one — the company's own site or filings over a directory aggregator — and note the disagreement in a comments column.

Where you cannot find a value, write Not found rather than an estimate, a rounded guess, or the value for a similar company. Where you found something but are not confident it is the right entity, write it and mark the row Low confidence.

Do not overwrite anything already in the sheet, even if you think it is wrong. Put the corrected value in a comments column and flag it for me.

Tell me at the end how many fields you filled, how many you could not, and which columns had the worst hit rate — that last one usually means the field is not publicly available and the column should be dropped.

templates.title: Pull a table from a page that blocks copy-paste
templates.outcome: A clean CSV of the table data that wouldn't let you select or copy it
templates.prompt:
There is a table at [URL] that I cannot select or copy out of. Get me the data.

Read the rendered page and extract the table's actual content — headers and every row. Work with what the page displays, and if the table is paginated or lazily rendered, page through it until you have everything rather than taking the visible rows.

Preserve the structure exactly: same columns in the same order, same number of rows, values as they appear. Do not reformat numbers, dates or currencies into what you think they should be — I will do that once I can see what the source actually said.

Where a cell is empty in the source, leave it empty. Where a cell holds a footnote marker, a link, or an icon rather than a value, capture what it means in a way I can act on rather than dropping it.

Write it to a Google Sheet.

Then tell me the row count and the column count so I can check them against what the page claims. If the table has a total or a subtotal row, keep it and label it rather than merging it into the data.

If the page turns out to be an image of a table rather than a table, say so — the accuracy of reading it is different and I need to know that before I use the numbers.

templates.title: Clean up my spreadsheet exactly how I tell you
templates.outcome: A tidy sheet — deduped, reformatted, and rule-checked without touching the rest
templates.prompt:
Clean up [sheet link] according to these rules and no others: [rules — e.g. dedupe on email, title-case names, phone numbers to E.164, trim whitespace, dates to YYYY-MM-DD, drop rows with no email].

Work on a copy, not the original. Name it [original name] — cleaned.

Apply exactly what I asked for. Do not also fix the things you notice that I did not mention, do not reorder columns, do not delete a column that looks empty, and do not "helpfully" normalise a field I did not name. A cleanup that quietly did more than it was told is one I have to diff against the original before I can use it, which costs more than doing it by hand.

Where a rule cannot be applied to a value — a phone number that is not a phone number, a date in a format the rule does not cover — leave the original value in place and add the row to an Exceptions tab with the field, the value, and which rule could not be applied. Those exceptions are usually the most interesting thing in the sheet.

When you dedupe, say which record you kept and why (most complete, most recent) and put the discarded duplicates on their own tab rather than deleting them.

Finish with a summary: rows in, rows out, per-rule counts of what changed, and how many exceptions.

templates.title: Merge my sheets into one and reconcile conflicts
templates.outcome: One master sheet with duplicates resolved and every conflict accounted for
templates.prompt:
Merge [sheet links] into one master sheet. The key that identifies the same record across them is [field].

First tell me what you are working with before merging anything: how many rows in each, which columns each has, and where the same concept is named differently across sheets. That mapping is the part that goes wrong, and I want to see it.

Match records on the key. Then for every field where two sources disagree about the same record, do not silently pick one. Write the master row using [precedence rule — e.g. the most recently updated sheet wins], and log the conflict to a Conflicts tab: the key, the field, each source's value, and which one was used.

The conflicts tab is the deliverable as much as the master sheet. A merged sheet with the disagreements hidden inside it is a sheet that looks authoritative and is not.

Records that appear in only one source go into the master with a column saying which source they came from.

Where the key is missing or duplicated within a single source, put those rows on an Unmatched tab rather than guessing.

Finish with the numbers: rows per source in, matched, merged, master total, conflicts logged, unmatched. If the totals do not reconcile, say so rather than presenting a number that does not add up.

templates.title: Turn this messy list into clean structured rows
templates.outcome: Structured, consistent rows you can paste anywhere, straight from raw text
templates.prompt:
Here is a messy list: [paste it, or a link]. Turn it into clean structured rows with these columns: [columns].

Read the whole thing first and work out its actual structure before parsing anything. Free-text lists usually have two or three inconsistent formats mixed together, and a parser tuned to the first ten lines mangles the rest.

Tell me what patterns you found and how you are splitting them, then do it.

For each entry, pull the fields into the columns. Normalise consistently: one date format, one phone format, consistent casing on names, URLs with a scheme. Keep the original raw text as the last column, so any row I doubt can be checked against what it came from without going back to the source.

Write it to a Google Sheet.

Where an entry does not fit the pattern, do not force it. Put it on an Unparsed tab with the raw text and a line on why. Ten unparsed rows I can fix by hand are much better than ten rows silently parsed into the wrong columns.

Where a field is genuinely absent from an entry, leave it empty rather than inferring it from the entries around it.

Finish with the counts: entries in, rows out, rows unparsed.

templates.title: Build a pricing comparison across competitor sites
templates.outcome: A side-by-side table of every competitor's plans, prices, and limits with sources
templates.prompt:
Build a side-by-side pricing comparison for [competitors].

Go to each one's actual pricing page. For every plan capture: plan name, monthly price, annual price and the effective monthly rate, what the plan includes, the limits that matter ([seats, usage, storage, API calls — whatever applies here]), and what is explicitly not included.

The limits are the point. Two products at $49 with a 10x difference in included usage are not competitors at the same price, and a table that shows only the headline number hides exactly the thing I need.

Also capture: whether there is a free tier and what it actually allows, whether pricing is public at all for the top tier, the currency, whether tax is included, minimum contract terms, and any per-seat minimum.

Write it as a table with plans as rows grouped by competitor, and the same fields as columns for all of them. Where a competitor does not have a comparable concept, write Not offered rather than leaving a blank that reads like missing data.

Every row gets the source URL and the date you checked. Pricing pages change and an undated comparison is worthless within a quarter.

Where pricing is "contact us", say that rather than estimating, and note anything you found about real prices in reviews separately and labelled as such.

templates.title: Watch a listings page and log new entries daily
templates.outcome: A sheet that quietly accumulates every new listing the moment it appears
templates.prompt:
Every morning, check [listings page URL] and append anything new to [sheet link].

New means not already in the sheet. Match on [a stable identifier — the listing URL or ID, never the title, which gets edited]. A job that reappears with a rewritten title is not a new job, and a sheet that thinks it is becomes useless within a fortnight.

For each new listing capture [fields], plus the URL and the date it was first seen. Keep the sheet append-only so the history stays intact and I can see how the listing volume changes over time.

Handle pagination properly — if listings are sorted newest first, you can stop once you hit ones already logged, but check a page beyond that in case the sort is not strictly chronological.

Also watch for listings that have disappeared since the last run and mark those rows Removed with the date, rather than deleting them. When something vanishes is often the most interesting thing in this kind of log.

Tell me each morning how many new, how many removed, and the total tracked. If the page structure has changed and you cannot parse it, say so loudly rather than appending zero rows — a scraper that silently returns nothing looks exactly like a quiet day.

templates.title: Track new job postings that match my criteria
templates.outcome: A daily-updated sheet of fresh, deduped job matches scored for fit
templates.prompt:
Every morning, check [job boards / company career pages] for new postings matching [titles], in [locations / remote], and add them to [sheet link].

De-duplicate hard. The same job appears on a company's own site, on LinkedIn, and on three aggregators, and a tracker full of the same role five times is one I stop opening. Match on company plus normalised title plus location, and keep the posting from the company's own site as the canonical one, with the other URLs in a column.

For each new posting: company, title, location and whether remote, posted date, comp range if stated, the canonical link, and a fit score out of 5 against my criteria at [link].

The fit score needs a one-line reason next to it, otherwise it is a number I cannot argue with. Score honestly — if most postings come out at 2, that tells me the search is too broad and that is worth knowing.

Flag anything scoring 4 or 5 at the top of the daily note so I see it the same day. For those roles, speed matters more than anything else this job does.

Skip staffing-agency reposts of a job already in the sheet from the employer directly. And where a posting has no comp and my state requires it, note that — it usually means the posting is old or out of state.

templates.title: Log prices for products I'm watching every day
templates.outcome: A price history sheet for your watchlist with drops called out as they happen
templates.prompt:
Every morning, check the price of each product in [sheet link] and log it.

For each row, open the product URL and read the current price. Capture: the date, the price, the currency, whether it is in stock, and any strike-through or was-price shown. Append as a new row in a history tab rather than overwriting — the history is the whole point, and a sheet that only holds today's price cannot tell me anything.

Be careful about which price you read. Product pages show a list price, a member price, a subscribe-and-save price, a price with a coupon applied and a price for a different variant, sometimes all at once. Read the price for the variant in my sheet, and record which one you took.

Call out changes in a summary each morning: anything that dropped, by how much and by what percent, anything that rose, anything that went out of stock or came back, and anything now at its lowest price since tracking started.

That last one is the reason this exists, so make it prominent.

If a page will not load or the product is gone, log that as the day's entry rather than skipping the row — a gap in a price history is indistinguishable from a day the job did not run.

templates.title: Extract fields from a batch of invoice PDFs
templates.outcome: Every invoice's key fields captured into your template, with iffy ones flagged
templates.prompt:
Read every invoice PDF in [Drive folder] and extract [fields — vendor, invoice number, date, due date, subtotal, tax, total, currency, PO number, line items] into [sheet link or a new sheet matching this template].

Invoices vary wildly in layout, so read each one properly rather than assuming a position. For each field, take the value the document actually states.

Then check your own work before writing the row: does the subtotal plus tax equal the total, does the sum of line items equal the subtotal, is the date plausible, is the currency what the symbol actually indicates. Where an internal check fails, still write the row but mark it Needs review with which check failed. Those are the ones worth my time and they are invisible in a sheet that presents every row with equal confidence.

Also flag: scanned or handwritten invoices where the read is uncertain, invoices in a currency other than [expected], duplicates of an invoice number already in the sheet, and anything with no total you could find.

Put the source filename and page in every row.

Do not round, do not convert currencies, and do not infer a missing tax amount by subtraction. Finish with counts: files read, rows written, rows flagged, files that could not be read at all.

templates.title: Turn last month's email receipts into an expense report
templates.outcome: A categorized monthly expense summary built from receipts sitting in your inbox
templates.prompt:
On the 1st of each month, go through my Gmail for last month and build an expense report from the receipts.

Search for receipts, invoices, order confirmations and payment notifications — including the ones that live in Promotions rather than the inbox, which is where half of them end up.

For each: date, merchant, amount, currency, what it was for, the payment method's last four if the email states it, and a link to the message. Categorise using [my categories, or: software, travel, meals, hardware, services, other].

Then the summary: total for the month, totals per category, the largest few line items, and a comparison against the previous month with anything that moved significantly called out.

Separate out two things that otherwise corrupt the total. Recurring subscriptions get their own section, so I can see the fixed base and spot the ones I forgot I was paying for. And anything that looks like a duplicate — same merchant, same amount, same day — gets flagged rather than counted twice, since an order confirmation and a receipt for the same purchase both look like charges.

Where an email is a quote, a renewal notice or a failed payment rather than an actual charge, leave it out and list those separately. This is a summary for me, not a filing; say plainly that the totals need checking against the card statement.

templates.title: Pull current rates from my affiliate dashboards
templates.outcome: One tracker showing every program's current rates, terms, and looming expirations
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, log into each affiliate dashboard listed in [sheet link] and pull the current terms into my tracker.

For each program capture: current commission rate and structure, cookie window, payout threshold, payment schedule, any tiered rates and what triggers the next tier, category exclusions, and the date of the most recent terms change if the dashboard shows one.

Compare against what the tracker already says and call out every difference. Rate changes are the reason this exists — programs cut rates quietly, the email goes to a shared inbox nobody reads, and the first sign is a month of lower revenue.

Flag separately anything with a deadline: promotional rates about to end, terms updates requiring acceptance, an account that will go inactive without a sale, or a payout threshold I am close to.

Also capture pending and paid balances if the dashboard shows them, so the tracker doubles as the answer to what I am owed.

Where a dashboard needs two-factor authentication you cannot complete, or the login fails, say which program and stop for that one — do not retry a login repeatedly, and do not skip it silently. A program missing from the update looks identical to a program with no changes.

templates.title: Build a shortlist of events worth attending
templates.outcome: A ranked list of conferences and events with dates, costs, and reasons to go
templates.prompt:
Build me a shortlist of events worth attending in [timeframe] for [purpose — selling, hiring, learning, visibility] in [industry / region].

For each: name, dates, city and venue, format, expected attendance, ticket cost including the early-bird deadline, and roughly what travel and hotel would add. The all-in number matters more than the ticket price and is the one every event page hides.

Then the part that decides it: who actually attends. Look at last year's speaker list, sponsor list and any published attendee breakdown, and say honestly whether the room contains the people I care about or whether it is mostly vendors selling to each other. A conference where the attendees are all sellers is a cost with no return, and it is common.

Also capture: whether the CFP is open and when it closes, whether sponsorship is worth it at the smallest tier, and what side events run alongside — the dinners and satellite meetups are frequently where the value is.

Rank by expected value for my stated purpose, and give each a one-line verdict: go, go only if speaking, sponsor rather than attend, or skip and why.

Include the skips with reasons. Knowing why not to go to the obvious big one is as useful as the shortlist.

templates.title: Mine product reviews for themes and quotes
templates.outcome: A breakdown of what customers praise and complain about, with receipts
templates.prompt:
Read the reviews of [product — ours or a competitor's] on G2 and Trustpilot and tell me what customers actually say.

Read across the rating distribution rather than just the extremes. The 3 and 4-star reviews are the most informative: they are written by people who use the thing and have specific grievances rather than an agenda.

Group what you find into themes, not a list of reviews. For each theme: what it is in one line, how many reviews raised it and out of how many read, whether it skews to a particular customer size or use case, and two or three verbatim quotes with the rating, the date and the link.

The quotes have to be exact. A paraphrased customer quote cannot be used in anything, and that is usually what this is for.

Split into praise and complaints, ordered by frequency within each. Then add a third section for the themes that changed over time — something complained about constantly in [older period] and rarely since is a fixed problem, and treating it as current makes us look uninformed.

Write it to a sheet with one row per quote so it stays searchable, plus the thematic summary above it.

Say how many reviews you read and over what period. A theme drawn from four reviews is not a theme, and I need to be able to tell.

templates.title: Diff two versions of a sheet and show what changed
templates.outcome: A change report listing every added, removed, and edited row between two versions
templates.prompt:
Compare [sheet A] against [sheet B] and tell me exactly what changed. The column that identifies a row across both is [key].

First check the shapes: row counts, column names, and any column present in one and not the other. A renamed column makes every row in it look changed, so establish the mapping before diffing anything.

Then produce a change report in a Google Doc with four sections:

Added — rows in B with a key not in A. Show the full row.
Removed — rows in A with a key not in B. Show the full row.
Changed — rows in both where any field differs. Show the key, the field, the old value and the new value, one line per changed field rather than per row.
Unchanged — the count only.

Call out separately anything structural: duplicated keys within either sheet, rows with a blank key, and columns added or dropped. Those are usually the real story and they get lost among a hundred value changes.

End with the counts, and check they reconcile: A total, B total, added, removed, changed, unchanged. If they do not add up, say so rather than presenting a report whose arithmetic does not work.

Do not modify either sheet.

templates.title: Source engineer candidates from GitHub activity
templates.outcome: A candidate sheet of active GitHub profiles matching your stack and location
templates.prompt:
Find engineers on GitHub who work with [languages / frameworks / domain] and are based in [location, or remote-friendly].

Search by contribution to relevant projects rather than by profile keywords — a bio saying "Rust" is worth nothing next to fifty merged PRs in a Rust project with real maintainers.

For each candidate capture: username and profile URL, name if public, location if public, current employer if stated, the specific evidence (which repos, what kind of contribution, merged or not, how recent), primary languages by actual code rather than by repo count, and activity over the last [12] months.

Separate signal from volume in what you report. Someone with four substantial merged PRs to a project that matters is a stronger candidate than someone with 2,000 commits to their own dotfiles, and the sheet should make that visible rather than sorting on a contribution count.

Add a LinkedIn URL where you can confidently match the person, and mark it uncertain where you cannot.

Write it to a Google Sheet ranked by strength of evidence.

Exclude anyone who works at [our company] or at [companies we do not approach]. Exclude accounts that are clearly bots or organisations. And do not include a personal email scraped from a commit — that is technically public and using it for recruiting is the fastest way to get a bad reputation among exactly the people we want.

templates.title: Summarize competitor product updates every week
templates.outcome: A Monday brief on every feature competitors shipped in the last week
templates.prompt:
Every Monday, check what [competitors] shipped in the last week and brief me on it.

Sources per competitor: their changelog or release notes, their blog, their docs (a new page in the docs often lands before any announcement), their status or roadmap page if public, and their product-related social posts.

For each shipped item: which competitor, what it is in plain terms, the date, the link, and what problem it solves for their users.

Then the part that makes this worth reading: what it means. Is it catching up to something we already do, is it a genuine gap opening between us, is it maintenance dressed up as news, or is it a signal about where they are heading? Say which, and say when you are not sure.

A lot of changelog content is noise, and a brief that reports every bug fix with equal weight buries the one thing that mattered. Rank by significance and put the trivia in a single line at the bottom.

If a competitor shipped nothing this week, say so in one line. A quiet quarter from a competitor is itself information.

And where something they shipped directly overlaps our roadmap, flag it clearly at the top — that is the item someone here needs to see the same day.

templates.title: Score vendors against my evaluation criteria
templates.outcome: A weighted scorecard comparing every vendor on the criteria you care about
templates.prompt:
Score [vendors] against my criteria: [criteria with weights, or the list and I will weight them].

For each vendor, research each criterion from their site, docs, pricing, status page, reviews and anything public about their security and compliance posture. Score each criterion, and put the evidence and its source next to the score. A scorecard whose numbers cannot be traced is one nobody can defend in the meeting where it gets used.

Build the table with vendors as columns and criteria as rows, weighted totals at the bottom.

Then the parts a score cannot hold:

Deal-breakers — anything that disqualifies a vendor regardless of total. A vendor missing a compliance requirement we must have does not get to win on features.

Unknowns — every criterion where you could not find out. List these explicitly per vendor rather than scoring them zero or average. "We could not determine this" and "they scored badly" are completely different and the total hides the difference.

Questions for each vendor's sales call, drawn from the unknowns.

Finish with a recommendation and, more usefully, what would have to be true for the runner-up to win instead. And say plainly if the scores are close enough that the ranking is not meaningful.

templates.title: Export my Amazon order history into a sheet
templates.outcome: Your full order history in one sheet with spend totals by month and category
templates.prompt:
Export my Amazon order history for [period] into a Google Sheet.

Go through the order history pages, paging back through the whole period. For each order capture: order date, order number, item name, quantity, item price, shipping, tax, order total, category if shown, and the order detail URL.

One row per item rather than per order, since an order with six items is six things I bought and the categorisation only works at the item level. Put the order number on each row so items can be grouped back.

Handle the awkward cases explicitly: cancelled and returned orders marked as such rather than counted as spend, digital orders and subscriptions separated out, and gift cards excluded from spend totals since they are a transfer rather than a purchase.

Then add a summary tab: total spend by month, by category, the largest orders, and the count of orders. Include the returns as a negative line rather than silently netting them off, so the gross and net are both visible.

If pagination breaks or a page will not load, say which date range is missing rather than handing me a total that is quietly short. A spend figure I believe and that is wrong is worse than no figure.

templates.title: Reconcile a bank statement to my books
templates.outcome: A clean reconciliation with every unmatched item flagged for review
templates.prompt:
Reconcile the bank statement at [file or Drive link] against my books at [sheet link] for [period].

Match on amount and date within a [3] day window, then on description where the amounts are ambiguous. Bank descriptions rarely match the payee name in the books, so expect to match on amount first and confirm on context.

Produce four sections:

Matched — transaction, date, amount, and both references. The count, not every line, unless I ask.

In the bank, not in the books — these are the ones that matter most. Full detail on each, with a guess at what it is where the description gives one.

In the books, not in the bank — outstanding cheques, timing differences, or entries that should not exist.

Amount mismatches — matched by date and payee but different amounts. Show both.

Then the reconciliation itself: opening balance per the bank, plus and minus the reconciling items, closing balance per the books, and the difference. State the difference plainly even when it is not zero — especially when it is not zero.

Do not force a match to make it balance, and do not adjust anything in either source. This is a reconciliation for a human to act on, not a set of corrections.

templates.title: Turn my transactions into a P&L
templates.outcome: Categorized income and expenses rolled up into a monthly P&L
templates.prompt:
Turn the transactions at [sheet or file link] into a monthly P&L.

Categorise every transaction using [my chart of accounts, or: revenue, cost of revenue, payroll, software, marketing, professional services, travel, office, other]. Put the category in a column next to each transaction rather than only in the summary, so the categorisation can be audited and corrected.

Where a transaction is ambiguous, put it in an Uncategorised bucket and list those separately. Do not spread them across plausible categories — an uncategorised total I can see is honest, and a P&L where 4% of spend was guessed into place is not.

Build the P&L by month: revenue, cost of revenue, gross profit and gross margin, then operating expenses by category, then operating profit. Add a total column for the period.

Call out anything that will distort a month: one-off charges, annual payments booked in the month they were paid, refunds, and transfers between my own accounts that are not income or expense at all. That last one inflates revenue in almost every DIY P&L I have seen.

This is a management view built from transaction data, not accounting output. Say so, and say which judgements you made that an accountant might make differently.

templates.title: Analyze my survey results
templates.outcome: Summary stats, cross-tabs, and open-text themes from a survey export
templates.prompt:
Analyse the survey export at [sheet link].

Start with the shape of it: how many responses, how many complete, the response period, and the drop-off by question. Then say plainly what that means for the rest — an analysis of 40 responses is a set of anecdotes with percentages on them, and the reader needs to know that before the first chart.

For each closed question: the distribution with counts and percentages, based on the number who answered that question rather than the total, and note where those differ.

Cross-tabs for the segments that matter: [segments — e.g. by plan, by tenure, by role]. Only report a cross-tab where the cell counts support it, and say the cell size. "70% of enterprise customers said X" over seven respondents is a sentence that will get repeated without the seven.

For open-text questions: read all of them and group into themes with counts and representative verbatim quotes. Quote exactly. Keep a residual Other with the count rather than forcing every response into a theme.

Finish with the three findings that are actually supported, and separately anything suggestive that would need more data. And note any question whose wording biases the answer — that belongs in the analysis, not in a footnote nobody reads.

templates.title: Build a cohort retention analysis
templates.outcome: Monthly cohorts with retention curves and the churn story behind them
templates.prompt:
Build a cohort retention analysis from the data at [sheet link]. Each row is [what a row is — a user, a subscription, an order] with [the signup/first-activity date field] and [the activity or renewal field].

Define the cohort by month of first activity, and define retained explicitly before you compute anything: [definition — e.g. had any activity in that month, or an active subscription on the last day of the month]. State the definition at the top of the output, because every retention number is meaningless without it and every argument about retention turns out to be an argument about the definition.

Build the triangle: cohorts as rows, months since signup as columns, both counts and percentages. Include the cohort size in the first column.

Then the reading of it:

Where the curve flattens, which is the number that actually matters — the floor is the business.
Whether recent cohorts are better or worse than older ones, and by how much.
Any cohort that behaves unlike its neighbours, with a guess at why (a pricing change, a campaign, a seasonal intake).

Grey out or omit the incomplete cells for recent cohorts rather than showing a partial month as a retention drop. That single artefact is the most common way a retention chart tells a story that is not true.

Write the tables to a sheet and the reading to a doc.

templates.title: Audit my store's catalog for sold-out and broken items
templates.outcome: A sweep of every product flagging sold-out, missing images, and price issues
templates.prompt:
Sweep every product in [store URL or product sheet] and flag what is broken.

For each product page check:

Availability — in stock, sold out, or unavailable, and for variant products, which specific variants are gone. A product that shows as available but where every size is sold out is the worst case, since it takes the customer to the last click before failing.

Images — missing, broken, placeholder, or fewer than [n]. Check the image actually loads rather than that the tag exists.

Price — missing, zero, obviously wrong (an order of magnitude off the category norm), sale price above the original, or a strike-through with no discount.

Content — empty or placeholder description, missing key attributes, a title that still says Copy or Draft.

Links — anything on the page that 404s.

Write it to a sheet, one row per issue rather than per product, with the product, the variant if relevant, the issue, the URL, and a severity. Sort by severity: a page that cannot be bought from first, a missing third image last.

Give me the totals by issue type at the top. And where the whole catalogue shows the same problem, say that as one line rather than as four hundred rows.
